items.stem: What is the name for "a ductless gland that secretes hormones directly into the blood"?
items.answer: Endocrine gland
items.markingKey: Endocrine gland: a ductless gland that secretes hormones directly into the blood.

items.stem: Explain how a high concentration of oestrogen causes ovulation.
items.answer: Rising oestrogen from the developing follicle has a positive feedback effect on the anterior pituitary (and hypothalamus), causing a surge in LH (and FSH), which causes the follicle to rupture and release the oocyte.
items.markingKey: positive feedback [1]; LH surge [1]; follicle ruptures [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why progesterone levels remain high if fertilisation occurs.
items.answer: The embryo secretes hCG, which maintains the corpus luteum, so it continues to secrete progesterone, keeping the endometrium for implantation.
items.markingKey: hCG from embryo [1]; corpus luteum maintained [1] [2]

items.stem: In a typical 28-day menstrual cycle, which event occurs at about day 21?
options: Menstruation; new follicles begin to develop
Corpus luteum degenerating; endometrium about to break down
items.answer: Corpus luteum active; endometrium maintained
items.markingKey: Day 21: corpus luteum active; endometrium maintained; progesterone at its peak.

items.stem: Felix is studying hormone data for a woman with a regular 28-day cycle. On day 14, the concentration of LH is at its peak. Explain the significance of this hormone level at this stage of the cycle.
items.answer: The LH surge causes the mature follicle to rupture and release the secondary oocyte (ovulation) and the follicle to become the corpus luteum.
items.markingKey: source gland/structure [1]; effect at this stage [1]; feedback link [1] [3]

items.stem: A health clinic in Dhaka is explaining how an emergency contraceptive containing a high dose of progesterone works to a group of students. (a) Explain why the pill must be taken at about the same time each day. (b) Describe the role of the hypothalamus in the menstrual cycle.
items.answer: (a) Synthetic hormones are broken down; regular doses keep their concentrations high enough to suppress FSH and LH. (b) It secretes GnRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH; it responds to oestrogen and progesterone feedback.
items.markingKey: (a) Synthetic hormones are broken down [1]; regular doses keep their concentrations high enough to suppress FSH and LH [1] [2] (b) It secretes GnRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH [1]; it responds to oestrogen and progesterone feedback [1] [2]

items.stem: Which hormone causes ovulation?
items.answer: LH
items.markingKey: A surge of LH around day 14 triggers ovulation.

items.stem: A blood test shows high progesterone and low FSH on day 21 of a cycle. What does this indicate?
options: An active corpus luteum is inhibiting FSH secretion
items.answer: An active corpus luteum is inhibiting FSH secretion
items.markingKey: Progesterone negative feedback.

items.stem: In a typical 28-day menstrual cycle, which event occurs at about day 10?
options: Menstruation; new follicles begin to develop
items.answer: Endometrium repaired and thickening
items.markingKey: Day 10: endometrium repaired and thickening; oestrogen rising to a peak.

items.stem: Omar is studying hormone data for a woman with a regular 28-day cycle. On day 21, the concentration of progesterone is at its peak. Explain the significance of this hormone level at this stage of the cycle.
items.answer: Progesterone from the corpus luteum maintains the endometrium for implantation and inhibits FSH/LH; its high level prevents new follicles developing.
items.markingKey: source gland/structure [1]; effect at this stage [1]; feedback link [1] [3]

items.stem: What is the name for "a rapid, temporary reversal of the potential difference across a neurone membrane, from −70 mV to about +30 mV"?
items.answer: Action potential
items.markingKey: Action potential: a rapid, temporary reversal of the potential difference across a neurone membrane, from −70 mV to about +30 mV.

items.stem: Explain how a resting potential is maintained.
items.answer: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump actively transports 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in; the membrane is more permeable to K⁺ (more K⁺ channels open), so K⁺ diffuse out; organic anions inside; inside is left negative at about −70 mV.
items.markingKey: pump 3 Na⁺ out 2 K⁺ in [1]; K⁺ leak out [1]; membrane less permeable to Na⁺ [1]; inside negative [1] [4]

items.stem: Describe the events that occur during an action potential.
items.answer: Stimulus causes some Na⁺ channels to open; threshold reached; many voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ diffuse in, depolarisation to +30 mV; Na⁺ channels close, K⁺ channels open, K⁺ diffuse out, repolarisation; hyperpolarisation; pump restores resting potential.
items.markingKey: threshold [1]; Na⁺ in / depolarisation [1]; K⁺ out / repolarisation [1]; hyperpolarisation and restoration [1] [4]

items.stem: Lucas stimulated a myelinated sensory neurone and recorded action potentials at two electrodes 50 cm apart. The action potential arrived at the second electrode 8.33 ms after the first. Explain why the action potential is not reduced in size as it travels along the axon.
items.answer: Each region of membrane generates a new full-sized action potential when it reaches threshold (all-or-nothing); energy comes from ion gradients along the axon.
items.markingKey: regenerated at each region [1]; all-or-nothing [1] [2]

items.stem: Sipho stimulated a myelinated sensory neurone and recorded action potentials at two electrodes 15 cm apart. The action potential arrived at the second electrode 1.88 ms after the first. (a) Calculate the conduction speed in m s⁻¹. (b) Explain why the action potential is not reduced in size as it travels along the axon.
items.answer: (a) 79.8 m s⁻¹ (b) Each region of membrane generates a new full-sized action potential when it reaches threshold (all-or-nothing); energy comes from ion gradients along the axon.
items.markingKey: (a) 15 cm = 0.15 m and 1.88 ms = 0.00188 s [1]; speed = 79.8 m s⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) regenerated at each region [1]; all-or-nothing [1] [2]

items.stem: Hana stimulated an unmyelinated C fibre and recorded action potentials at two electrodes 2 cm apart. The action potential arrived at the second electrode 14.29 ms after the first. (a) Calculate the conduction speed in m s⁻¹. (b) Explain why this speed is low compared with other neurones.
items.answer: (a) 1.40 m s⁻¹ (b) The axon is unmyelinated and narrow, so depolarisation must occur along the whole membrane by local circuits.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 cm = 0.02 m and 14.29 ms = 0.01429 s [1]; speed = 1.40 m s⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) myelination / diameter linked to speed [2]

items.stem: In the effect of a local anaesthetic such as lidocaine, the drug blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in sensory neurones. (a) Explain how the resting potential is restored after an action potential. (b) Explain why neurones contain many mitochondria.
items.answer: (a) K⁺ diffuse out through K⁺ channels (repolarisation); Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in to restore the ion concentrations. (b) ATP is needed for the Na⁺/K⁺ pump to maintain the resting potential and for vesicle movement/neurotransmitter synthesis at synapses.
items.markingKey: (a) K⁺ out [1]; pump restores gradients [1] [2] (b) ATP is needed for the Na⁺/K⁺ pump to maintain the resting potential and for vesicle movement/neurotransmitter synthesis at synapses [2] [2]

items.stem: In the effect of a local anaesthetic such as lidocaine, the drug blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in sensory neurones. (a) Explain the effect on the transmission of nerve impulses. (b) Explain how the resting potential is restored after an action potential.
items.answer: (a) Action potentials cannot be generated or conducted in sensory neurones, so impulses from pain receptors do not reach the brain. (b) K⁺ diffuse out through K⁺ channels (repolarisation); Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in to restore the ion concentrations.
items.markingKey: (a) Action potentials cannot be generated or conducted in sensory neurones, so impulses from pain receptors do not reach the brain. [3] (b) K⁺ out [1]; pump restores gradients [1] [2]

items.stem: Which ions diffuse into the axon during depolarisation?
items.answer: Sodium ions
items.markingKey: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open.

items.stem: A neurone has a refractory period of 2 ms. What is the maximum frequency of impulses it can carry?
items.answer: 500 Hz
items.markingKey: 1 ÷ 0.002 s = 500 per second.

items.stem: Explain why action potentials are described as all-or-nothing.
items.answer: If threshold is reached an action potential of the same size (+30 mV) is always produced; below threshold none is produced; stimulus strength is coded by frequency of impulses, not size.
items.markingKey: same size if threshold reached [1]; none below [1]; frequency codes intensity [1] [3]

items.stem: A trace of an action potential recorded by Lina shows a stage in which the potential returns to −70 mV. Explain the changes in ion movement responsible.
items.answer: K⁺ channels close; the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and leak channels restore the resting potential.
items.markingKey: K⁺ channels close; the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and leak channels restore the resting potential [2]

items.stem: Explain how a resting potential is maintained and how an action potential is produced and transmitted along a myelinated neurone.
items.answer: Na⁺/K⁺ pump 3:2; K⁺ leak; −70 mV; stimulus → threshold; voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ in, +30 mV; K⁺ channels open, K⁺ out; hyperpolarisation; refractory period; local circuits; myelin by Schwann cells insulates; saltatory conduction node to node; faster; all-or-nothing; one direction.
items.markingKey: resting potential [2]; depolarisation [1]; repolarisation / hyperpolarisation [1]; refractory period [1]; local circuits [1]; saltatory conduction [1] [7]

items.stem: Which term is defined as "the combined effect of several excitatory postsynaptic potentials, from one or more presynaptic neurones, that together reach threshold"?
items.answer: Summation
items.markingKey: Summation: the combined effect of several excitatory postsynaptic potentials, from one or more presynaptic neurones, that together reach threshold.

items.stem: Describe how an impulse is transmitted across a cholinergic synapse.
items.answer: Action potential arrives at presynaptic knob; voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open, Ca²⁺ diffuse in; vesicles move and fuse with presynaptic membrane, releasing ACh by exocytosis; ACh diffuses across cleft and binds to receptors; Na⁺ channels open, depolarisation; if threshold reached, action potential; ACh hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase; choline reabsorbed.
items.markingKey: Ca²⁺ in [1]; exocytosis of ACh [1]; diffusion and binding to receptors [1]; Na⁺ in, depolarisation [1]; ACh hydrolysed and recycled [1] [5]

items.stem: Explain why acetylcholine must be broken down quickly after it has bound to its receptors.
items.answer: Otherwise Na⁺ channels would stay open and the postsynaptic membrane would remain depolarised, causing continuous impulses (e.g. sustained muscle contraction) and preventing new signals.
items.markingKey: channels stay open / continuous depolarisation [1]; consequence [1] [2]

items.stem: Freya reads that botulinum toxin prevents the release of acetylcholine from vesicles. Predict and explain the effect on synaptic transmission.
items.answer: No ACh released so no depolarisation of the muscle; muscles are paralysed.
items.markingKey: effect on ACh / receptors [1]; effect on postsynaptic membrane [1]; consequence for muscle / neurone [1] [3]

items.stem: An organophosphate insecticide inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Explain the effect of an organophosphate insecticide on transmission at a neuromuscular junction.
items.answer: ACh is not broken down, so postsynaptic Na⁺ channels stay open; continuous depolarisation causes sustained contraction / spasms and paralysis.
items.markingKey: effect on ACh / receptors [1]; effect on postsynaptic membrane [1]; consequence for muscle / neurone [1] [3]

items.stem: Alzheimer's disease, in which cholinergic neurones in the brain are lost and acetylcholine levels fall. Doctors in Bogotá treat it with an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. (a) Explain the symptoms of the condition in terms of synaptic transmission. (b) Suggest a possible side effect of the treatment.
items.answer: (a) Less acetylcholine is released, so postsynaptic neurones are depolarised less often; transmission in memory pathways fails. (b) Excess stimulation at other cholinergic synapses (e.g. muscle twitching, slow heart rate, excess salivation).
items.markingKey: (a) link to receptors / ACh amount [1]; less depolarisation [1]; consequence [1] [3] (b) Excess stimulation at other cholinergic synapses (e.g. muscle twitching, slow heart rate, excess salivation) [1]

items.stem: Explain why the presynaptic knob contains many mitochondria.
items.answer: ATP is needed to resynthesise acetylcholine from choline and acetyl CoA, to move vesicles and to pump Ca²⁺ back out.
items.markingKey: ATP for synthesis of ACh [1]; for vesicle transport / Ca²⁺ pumping [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how summation at synapses allows integration of information.
items.answer: A single presynaptic impulse may release too little transmitter to reach threshold; several impulses in quick succession (temporal) or from several neurones (spatial) add together; inhibitory synapses can cancel excitatory ones.
items.markingKey: temporal [1]; spatial [1]; inhibition / integration [1] [3]

items.stem: Nicotine binds to and opens acetylcholine receptors (an agonist). What is the effect at a cholinergic synapse?
options: ACh is not broken down, so postsynaptic Na⁺ channels stay open; continuous depolarisation causes sustained contraction / spasms and paralysis
ACh cannot bind so muscle fibres are not depolarised; paralysis, including breathing muscles
ACh cannot bind, so no depolarisation of the muscle fibre; flaccid paralysis
Mimics ACh, causing depolarisation of postsynaptic neurones even without ACh
items.answer: Mimics ACh, causing depolarisation of postsynaptic neurones even without ACh
items.markingKey: Mimics ACh, causing depolarisation of postsynaptic neurones even without ACh.

items.stem: Describe the structure of a cholinergic synapse and explain how an impulse is transmitted across it.
items.answer: Presynaptic knob, mitochondria, vesicles, Ca²⁺ channels; cleft; postsynaptic receptors, AChE. Action potential → Ca²⁺ in → vesicles fuse → exocytosis of ACh → diffuses → binds receptors → Na⁺ channels open → EPSP → threshold → action potential; ACh hydrolysed; choline reabsorbed, ACh resynthesised with ATP; one-way.
items.markingKey: structure [2]; Ca²⁺ and exocytosis [1]; diffusion and binding [1]; depolarisation / threshold [1]; breakdown and recycling [1]; one-way transmission [1] [7]

items.stem: Which term is defined as "an infolding of the sarcolemma that carries depolarisation deep into the muscle fibre"?
items.answer: T-tubule
items.markingKey: T-tubule: an infolding of the sarcolemma that carries depolarisation deep into the muscle fibre.

items.stem: Describe the sliding filament model of muscle contraction.
items.answer: Ca²⁺ binds to troponin, moving tropomyosin to expose binding sites on actin; myosin heads bind forming cross-bridges; heads tilt (power stroke) pulling actin towards the centre of the sarcomere, releasing ADP and Pi; ATP binds, heads detach; ATP hydrolysed, heads re-cock and bind further along; filaments slide, sarcomere shortens.
items.markingKey: Ca²⁺ / troponin / tropomyosin [1]; cross-bridges [1]; power stroke [1]; ATP detaches / recocks [1]; filaments slide, not shorten [1] [5]

items.stem: Explain how an action potential at the neuromuscular junction leads to the release of calcium ions inside the muscle fibre.
items.answer: ACh depolarises the sarcolemma; the action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and down T-tubules; this causes Ca²⁺ channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum to open; Ca²⁺ diffuse into the sarcoplasm.
items.markingKey: sarcolemma depolarised [1]; T-tubules [1]; SR releases Ca²⁺ [1] [3]

items.stem: In a myofibril studied by Mateo, each myosin filament is 1.6 μm long and each actin filament extends 0.95 μm from the Z line. A relaxed sarcomere is 3.1 μm long; when contracted it is 2.5 μm long. State the width of the A band in the contracted sarcomere and explain your answer.
items.answer: 1.6 μm; the myosin filaments do not shorten, so the A band stays the same.
items.markingKey: value [1]; myosin unchanged [1] [2]

items.stem: In a myofibril studied by Tomás, each myosin filament is 1.6 μm long and each actin filament extends 0.95 μm from the Z line. A relaxed sarcomere is 3.1 μm long; when contracted it is 2.3 μm long. (a) State the width of the A band in the contracted sarcomere and explain your answer. (b) Calculate the percentage decrease in sarcomere length.
items.answer: (a) 1.6 μm; the myosin filaments do not shorten, so the A band stays the same. (b) 25.8%

items.stem: A researcher in Jakarta treated isolated muscle fibres with a drug that prevents the reuptake of calcium ions into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. (a) Explain why myofibrils contract only when both ATP and calcium ions are present. (b) Explain the role of creatine phosphate in muscle.
items.answer: (a) Ca²⁺ is needed to move tropomyosin and expose myosin-binding sites on actin; ATP is needed for the myosin heads to detach and re-cock so that cycling continues. (b) It donates a phosphate group to ADP to regenerate ATP rapidly during intense activity.
items.markingKey: (a) role of Ca²⁺ [1]; role of ATP [1] [2] (b) It donates a phosphate group to ADP to regenerate ATP rapidly during intense activity [2] [2]

items.stem: Explain why rigor mortis occurs after death.
items.answer: Without respiration no ATP is made; myosin heads cannot detach from actin, so cross-bridges stay attached and the muscles remain rigid.
items.markingKey: no ATP [1]; heads cannot detach [1] [2]

items.stem: In a myofibril studied by Tariq, each myosin filament is 1.6 μm long and each actin filament extends 0.95 μm from the Z line. A relaxed sarcomere is 2.7 μm long; when contracted it is 2.3 μm long. Calculate the total width of the I band (both halves) in the relaxed sarcomere.
items.answer: 1.1 μm
items.markingKey: I band = sarcomere − A band = 2.7 − 1.6 [1] = 1.1 μm [1] [2]

items.stem: In a myofibril studied by Ines, each myosin filament is 1.5 μm long and each actin filament extends 0.95 μm from the Z line. A relaxed sarcomere is 3.1 μm long; when contracted it is 2.7 μm long. (a) Calculate the total width of the I band (both halves) in the relaxed sarcomere. (b) State the width of the A band in the contracted sarcomere and explain your answer. (c) Calculate the percentage decrease in sarcomere length.
items.answer: (a) 1.6 μm (b) 1.5 μm; the myosin filaments do not shorten, so the A band stays the same. (c) 12.9%
items.markingKey: (a) I band = sarcomere − A band = 3.1 − 1.5 [1] = 1.6 μm [1] [2] (b) value [1]; myosin unchanged [1] [2] (c) (3.1 − 2.7) ÷ 3.1 × 100 = 12.9% [1]

items.stem: Describe the structure of a sarcomere and explain how a muscle fibre contracts.
items.answer: Z lines, actin thin filaments, myosin thick filaments; A band, I band, H zone, M line; neuromuscular junction ACh → depolarisation of sarcolemma → T-tubules → SR releases Ca²⁺ → troponin → tropomyosin moves → cross-bridges → power stroke (ADP + Pi released) → ATP binds, detach → ATP hydrolysed, recock → sliding; relaxation: Ca²⁺ pumped back.
items.markingKey: sarcomere structure [2]; excitation to Ca²⁺ release [2]; troponin/tropomyosin [1]; cross-bridge cycle [2]; relaxation [1] [8]

items.stem: Which term is defined as "a protein activated at low pH that loosens the links between cellulose microfibrils in a plant cell wall"?
items.answer: Expansin
items.markingKey: Expansin: a protein activated at low pH that loosens the links between cellulose microfibrils in a plant cell wall.

items.stem: Which term is defined as "a plant hormone that causes stem elongation and stimulates the breakdown of starch stores during seed germination"?
items.answer: Gibberellin
items.markingKey: Gibberellin: a plant hormone that causes stem elongation and stimulates the breakdown of starch stores during seed germination.

items.stem: Explain how the leaves of a Venus fly trap close rapidly.
items.answer: Touching sensory hairs opens ion channels, generating receptor potentials and an action potential; two action potentials within about 20 s trigger rapid movement of ions and water in the hinge cells (and acid growth of outer cells), so the leaf changes shape from convex to concave and snaps shut.
items.markingKey: hairs touched, action potential [1]; two needed [1]; ion and water movement / turgor change [1]; shape change snaps shut [1] [4]

items.stem: Priya floated 10 mm sections cut from wheat coleoptiles in solutions of different auxin (IAA) concentrations for 24 hours in the dark, then measured their final lengths. Results table. IAA concentration / mg dm⁻³: 0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10. Mean increase in length / mm, trial 1: 0.7, 0.9, 1.9, 4.6, 4.5, 1.9; trial 2: 0.8, 0.9, 1.9, 4.5, 4.6, 1.8; trial 3: 0.8, 0.9, 1.8, 4.5, 4.5, 1.8. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: Independent: IAA concentration; dependent: mean increase in length.
items.markingKey: independent variable = IAA concentration [1]; dependent variable = mean increase in length [1] [2]

items.stem: Lina floated 10 mm sections cut from wheat coleoptiles in solutions of different auxin (IAA) concentrations for 24 hours in the dark, then measured their final lengths. Results table. IAA concentration / mg dm⁻³: 0, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100. Mean increase in length / mm, trial 1: 0.9, 1.9, 4.8, 4.9, 2, 1; trial 2: 0.9, 2, 5, 5, 1.9, 0.9; trial 3: 0.8, 2.1, 5.1, 4.8, 2, 1. (a) Suggest one way to improve this investigation. (b) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) Use more sections per concentration. (b) A line graph: IAA concentration on the x-axis and mean mean increase in length on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) Any one from: use more sections per concentration; measure with a ruler under a magnifying lens or use image analysis; remove the tips so the coleoptile does not produce its own auxin; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the IAA concentration (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1] (b) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; IAA concentration on x-axis and mean increase in length on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Ethan floated 10 mm sections cut from wheat coleoptiles in solutions of different auxin (IAA) concentrations for 24 hours in the dark, then measured their final lengths. Results table. IAA concentration / mg dm⁻³: 0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10. Mean increase in length / mm, trial 1: 0.9, 1, 2.1, 5.4, 5.3, 2.2; trial 2: 0.9, 1, 2.2, 3, 5.1, 2.2; trial 3: 0.9, 1, 2.2, 5.1, 5.2, 2.2. (a) Suggest one way to improve this investigation. (b) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) Use more sections per concentration. (b) A line graph: IAA concentration on the x-axis and mean mean increase in length on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) Any one from: use more sections per concentration; measure with a ruler under a magnifying lens or use image analysis; remove the tips so the coleoptile does not produce its own auxin; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the IAA concentration (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1] (b) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; IAA concentration on x-axis and mean increase in length on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Jonas floated 10 mm sections cut from wheat coleoptiles in solutions of different auxin (IAA) concentrations for 24 hours in the dark, then measured their final lengths. Results table. IAA concentration / mg dm⁻³: 0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10. Mean increase in length / mm, trial 1: 0.9, 1, 2.1, 5.1, 5.1, 2.2; trial 2: 0.9, 1, 2.2, 5.2, 5, 3.2; trial 3: 0.9, 1, 2.2, 5.3, 5.1, 2. (a) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation. (b) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (c) Calculate the mean mean increase in length at 0 mg dm⁻³, ignoring any anomalous result.

items.stem: Which structure secretes progesterone in the second half of the menstrual cycle?
items.answer: Corpus luteum
items.markingKey: The corpus luteum develops from the ruptured follicle.

items.stem: Explain the roles of negative feedback in the control of the menstrual cycle.
items.answer: Progesterone (and oestrogen) from the corpus luteum inhibit FSH and LH secretion, so no new follicles develop; when the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, FSH rises again and a new cycle starts.
items.markingKey: progesterone inhibits FSH/LH [1]; no new follicles [1]; fall allows new cycle [1] [3]

items.stem: In a typical 28-day menstrual cycle, which event occurs at about day 21?
options: Corpus luteum degenerating; endometrium about to break down
items.answer: Corpus luteum active; endometrium maintained
items.markingKey: Day 21: corpus luteum active; endometrium maintained; progesterone at its peak.

items.stem: Describe the hormonal control of the human menstrual cycle and explain how the contraceptive pill prevents pregnancy.
items.answer: GnRH; FSH stimulates follicle growth and oestrogen; oestrogen repairs endometrium, inhibits FSH, then high oestrogen positive feedback → LH surge → ovulation day 14; corpus luteum secretes progesterone, maintains endometrium, inhibits FSH/LH; degenerates → progesterone falls → menstruation; pill: synthetic oestrogen/progesterone, negative feedback, no FSH/LH, no ovulation.
items.markingKey: FSH and follicles [1]; oestrogen effects [1]; LH surge and ovulation [1]; corpus luteum and progesterone [1]; menstruation [1]; pill mechanism [2] [7]

items.stem: What is the approximate resting potential of a neurone?
items.answer: −70 mV
items.markingKey: Inside negative relative to outside.

items.stem: Explain how local circuits cause an action potential to move along an unmyelinated axon.
items.answer: Na⁺ that enter at the depolarised region diffuse sideways along the axon; this depolarises the next region to threshold, opening its Na⁺ channels; the region behind is refractory so the impulse moves forwards.
items.markingKey: Na⁺ diffuse sideways [1]; next region reaches threshold [1]; refractory behind [1] [3]

items.stem: Samuel stimulated an unmyelinated C fibre and recorded action potentials at two electrodes 0.5 cm apart. The action potential arrived at the second electrode 8.33 ms after the first. Calculate the conduction speed in m s⁻¹.
On an oscilloscope trace of an action potential, at stage C the potential falls from +30 mV to −70 mV. Explain what is happening to ion channels at this stage.
items.answer: Na⁺ channels close; voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ diffuse out (repolarisation).
items.markingKey: Na⁺ channels close; voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ diffuse out (repolarisation) [2]

items.stem: Tomás stimulated a squid giant axon and recorded action potentials at two electrodes 80 cm apart. The action potential arrived at the second electrode 44.44 ms after the first. (a) Explain why this speed is high compared with other neurones. (b) The refractory period of this neurone is 5 ms. Calculate the maximum frequency of action potentials.
items.answer: (a) The giant axon has a very large diameter, which reduces resistance and increases local circuit spread; it is not myelinated. (b) 200 Hz
items.markingKey: (a) myelination / diameter linked to speed [2] (b) 1 ÷ 0.005 s = 200 impulses per second [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "acetylcholine"?
options: The enzyme in the synaptic cleft that hydrolyses acetylcholine into choline and ethanoic acid (acetate).
A synapse between a motor neurone and a muscle fibre.
The gap of about 20 nm between the presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes.
The neurotransmitter released at cholinergic synapses and neuromuscular junctions.
items.answer: The neurotransmitter released at cholinergic synapses and neuromuscular junctions.
items.markingKey: Acetylcholine: the neurotransmitter released at cholinergic synapses and neuromuscular junctions.

items.stem: Kwame writes in a revision note: "Acetylcholine enters the postsynaptic neurone to cause depolarisation." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Acetylcholine binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane; the opening of Na⁺ channels causes depolarisation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Acetylcholine binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane; the opening of Na⁺ channels causes depolarisation. [2]

items.stem: A reflex pathway in an experimental animal contains 4 synapses and a total neurone length of 6 cm. Impulses travel along the neurones at 20 m s⁻¹, and the delay at each synapse is 0.4 ms. (a) Calculate the percentage of the total time taken by synaptic transmission. (b) Suggest why reflex arcs have few synapses.
items.answer: (a) 35% (b) Fewer synapses means less synaptic delay so the response is faster, protecting the body from harm.
items.markingKey: (a) 1.6 ÷ 4.6 × 100 = 35% [1] (b) Fewer synapses means less synaptic delay so the response is faster, protecting the body from harm [1]

items.stem: Alzheimer's disease, in which cholinergic neurones in the brain are lost and acetylcholine levels fall. Doctors in Riyadh treat it with an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. (a) Explain the symptoms of the condition in terms of synaptic transmission. (b) Explain how the treatment helps.
items.answer: (a) Less acetylcholine is released, so postsynaptic neurones are depolarised less often; transmission in memory pathways fails. (b) Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase means acetylcholine stays in the cleft longer and at a higher concentration, so it binds to the remaining receptors more often and depolarisation is more likely to reach threshold.
items.markingKey: (a) link to receptors / ACh amount [1]; less depolarisation [1]; consequence [1] [3] (b) ACh not hydrolysed [1]; stays longer / more binding [1]; threshold reached [1] [3]

items.stem: A sarcomere contracts from 2.8 μm to 2.2 μm. Which band stays the same width?
items.answer: A band
items.markingKey: Myosin filaments do not shorten.

items.stem: Explain why muscle fibres contain many mitochondria.
items.answer: Large amounts of ATP are needed for detaching and re-cocking myosin heads and for pumping Ca²⁺ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
items.markingKey: ATP for cross-bridge cycling [1]; for Ca²⁺ pumping [1] [2]

items.stem: In a myofibril studied by Ethan, each myosin filament is 1.6 μm long and each actin filament extends 0.95 μm from the Z line. A relaxed sarcomere is 3 μm long; when contracted it is 2.1 μm long. State the width of the A band in the contracted sarcomere and explain your answer.
items.answer: 1.6 μm; the myosin filaments do not shorten, so the A band stays the same.
items.markingKey: value [1]; myosin unchanged [1] [2]

items.stem: Isolated myofibrils in Doha were placed in solutions with and without ATP and calcium ions, and their lengths were observed under a microscope. (a) Predict and explain the effect of preventing reuptake of calcium ions into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. (b) Describe how the appearance of a sarcomere differs between relaxed and contracted states in electron micrographs.
items.answer: (a) The muscle would stay contracted: Ca²⁺ stays bound to troponin, binding sites remain exposed and cross-bridges keep forming as long as ATP is available. (b) Contracted: Z lines closer, I band narrower, H zone narrower or absent, A band unchanged.
items.markingKey: (a) stays contracted [1]; Ca²⁺ stays bound to troponin [1]; binding sites exposed [1] [3] (b) I band [1]; H zone [1]; A band unchanged [1] [3]

items.stem: Gibberellin is applied to a dwarf pea variety. What is the expected result?
options: The stems elongate to normal height
items.answer: The stems elongate to normal height
items.markingKey: Dwarf varieties lack active gibberellin.

items.stem: Yusuf floated 10 mm sections cut from wheat coleoptiles in solutions of different auxin (IAA) concentrations for 24 hours in the dark, then measured their final lengths. Results table. IAA concentration / mg dm⁻³: 0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10. Mean increase in length / mm, trial 1: 0.8, 0.9, 1.9, 4.7, 4.8, 1.9; trial 2: 0.8, 0.9, 2, 4.7, 4.8, 1.9; trial 3: 1.2, 0.9, 1.9, 4.9, 4.9, 2. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: Independent: IAA concentration; dependent: mean increase in length.
items.markingKey: independent variable = IAA concentration [1]; dependent variable = mean increase in length [1] [2]

items.stem: Mei floated 10 mm sections cut from wheat coleoptiles in solutions of different auxin (IAA) concentrations for 24 hours in the dark, then measured their final lengths. Results table. IAA concentration / mg dm⁻³: 0, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100. Mean increase in length / mm, trial 1: 0.8, 2.1, 5.2, 5.1, 2.1, 0.6; trial 2: 0.8, 2.1, 5.1, 5, 2.1, 0.9; trial 3: 0.9, 2.2, 5.1, 5.1, 2, 1. (a) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (b) Describe a suitable control for this investigation and explain why it is needed.
items.answer: (a) Trial 1 at 100 mg dm⁻³ (0.6 mm); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) Sections in buffer solution with no IAA, showing the growth without added auxin.
items.markingKey: (a) trial 1 at 100 mg dm⁻³ identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2] (b) 1 mark: control described; 1 mark: shows that the change is caused by the independent variable [2]

items.stem: How does the combined contraceptive pill prevent pregnancy?
options: It kills sperm in the vagina
Oestrogen and progesterone inhibit FSH and LH secretion so no follicles develop and no ovulation occurs
items.answer: Oestrogen and progesterone inhibit FSH and LH secretion so no follicles develop and no ovulation occurs
items.markingKey: Negative feedback on the pituitary.

items.stem: Which hormone surge is detected by an ovulation test kit?
items.answer: LH
items.markingKey: LH surge precedes ovulation by about 24–36 h.

items.stem: In a typical 28-day menstrual cycle, which event occurs at about day 3?
options: Menstruation; new follicles begin to develop
Corpus luteum degenerating; endometrium about to break down
items.answer: Menstruation; new follicles begin to develop
items.markingKey: Day 3: menstruation; new follicles begin to develop; FSH low-moderate and rising.

items.stem: A health clinic in Lagos is explaining how a progesterone-only pill works to a group of students. (a) Explain how this pill prevents pregnancy. (b) Suggest one social or ethical issue linked to the use of oral contraceptives. (c) Describe the role of the hypothalamus in the menstrual cycle.
items.answer: (a) The synthetic hormones inhibit FSH and LH secretion by the anterior pituitary (negative feedback), so follicles do not mature and there is no LH surge or ovulation; progesterone also thickens cervical mucus. (b) Allows control of family size / women's careers; side effects and health risks (e.g. thrombosis); religious objections; no protection against STIs. (c) It secretes GnRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH; it responds to oestrogen and progesterone feedback.
items.markingKey: (a) inhibits FSH/LH [1]; no follicle development/ovulation [1]; cervical mucus [1] [3] (b) any 2 from: Allows control of family size / women's careers; side effects and health risks (e.g. thrombosis); religious objections; no protection against STIs (1 mark each) [2] (c) It secretes GnRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH [1]; it responds to oestrogen and progesterone feedback [1] [2]

items.stem: How many sodium and potassium ions are moved by one cycle of the sodium–potassium pump?
items.answer: 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in
items.markingKey: Uses one ATP per cycle.

items.stem: Explain how saltatory conduction increases the speed of transmission.
items.answer: Myelin insulates the axon so depolarisation occurs only at nodes of Ranvier; local circuits extend from node to node, so the impulse jumps and fewer depolarisations are needed.
items.markingKey: myelin insulates [1]; action potentials only at nodes [1]; jumps / fewer depolarisations [1] [3]

items.stem: A trace of an action potential recorded by Mei shows a stage in which the potential rises rapidly from −50 mV to +30 mV. Explain the changes in ion movement responsible.
items.answer: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open; Na⁺ diffuse in rapidly down their electrochemical gradient (depolarisation).
items.markingKey: voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open; Na⁺ diffuse in rapidly down their electrochemical gradient (depolarisation) [2]

items.stem: On an oscilloscope trace of an action potential, at stage D the potential falls below −70 mV to about −80 mV. Explain what is happening to ion channels at this stage.
items.answer: K⁺ channels are slow to close so too many K⁺ leave (hyperpolarisation).
items.markingKey: K⁺ channels are slow to close so too many K⁺ leave (hyperpolarisation) [2]

items.stem: Priya stimulated a myelinated motor neurone and recorded action potentials at two electrodes 80 cm apart. The action potential arrived at the second electrode 8.51 ms after the first. (a) Calculate the conduction speed in m s⁻¹. (b) Explain why this speed is high compared with other neurones.
items.answer: (a) 94.0 m s⁻¹ (b) The axon is myelinated (saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier) and/or has a large diameter.
items.markingKey: (a) 80 cm = 0.8 m and 8.51 ms = 0.00851 s [1]; speed = 94.0 m s⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) myelination / diameter linked to speed [2]

items.stem: State the products of hydrolysis of acetylcholine.
items.answer: Choline and ethanoic acid (acetate).
items.markingKey: Choline and ethanoic acid (acetate) [1]

items.stem: A student in Lima states: "The action potential jumps across the synaptic cleft." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Transmission across the cleft is chemical: neurotransmitter diffuses across and binds to receptors.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Transmission across the cleft is chemical: neurotransmitter diffuses across and binds to receptors. [2]

items.stem: A reflex pathway in an experimental animal contains 4 synapses and a total neurone length of 6 cm. Impulses travel along the neurones at 50 m s⁻¹, and the delay at each synapse is 0.5 ms. Explain why transmission across a synapse is slower than conduction along an axon.
items.answer: Transmission involves several steps: Ca²⁺ entry, exocytosis, diffusion of ACh across the cleft and binding to receptors before depolarisation.
items.markingKey: chemical steps listed [1]; diffusion is slow [1] [2]

items.stem: Alzheimer's disease, in which cholinergic neurones in the brain are lost and acetylcholine levels fall. Doctors in Accra treat it with an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. (a) Explain the symptoms of the condition in terms of synaptic transmission. (b) Describe the structure of a cholinergic synapse.
items.answer: (a) Less acetylcholine is released, so postsynaptic neurones are depolarised less often; transmission in memory pathways fails. (b) Presynaptic knob with mitochondria, vesicles of ACh, voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; synaptic cleft ~20 nm; postsynaptic membrane with ACh receptors (ligand-gated Na⁺ channels) and acetylcholinesterase.
items.markingKey: (a) link to receptors / ACh amount [1]; less depolarisation [1]; consequence [1] [3] (b) presynaptic features [1]; cleft [1]; postsynaptic receptors / enzyme [1] [3]

items.stem: Which event directly causes the myosin head to detach from actin?
options: ATP binding to the myosin head
items.answer: ATP binding to the myosin head
items.markingKey: ATP binding reduces affinity for actin.

items.stem: Mohammed says: "ATP is needed for the myosin head to attach to actin." Explain whether Mohammed is correct.
items.answer: Attachment needs exposed binding sites (Ca²⁺); ATP is needed for the head to detach and to re-cock.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Attachment needs exposed binding sites (Ca²⁺); ATP is needed for the head to detach and to re-cock. [2]

items.stem: In a myofibril studied by Priya, each myosin filament is 1.5 μm long and each actin filament extends 0.95 μm from the Z line. A relaxed sarcomere is 3.1 μm long; when contracted it is 2.4 μm long. State the width of the A band in the contracted sarcomere and explain your answer.
items.answer: 1.5 μm; the myosin filaments do not shorten, so the A band stays the same.
items.markingKey: value [1]; myosin unchanged [1] [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Singapore treated isolated muscle fibres with a drug that prevents the reuptake of calcium ions into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. (a) Predict and explain the effect of preventing reuptake of calcium ions into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. (b) Describe how the appearance of a sarcomere differs between relaxed and contracted states in electron micrographs.
items.answer: (a) The muscle would stay contracted: Ca²⁺ stays bound to troponin, binding sites remain exposed and cross-bridges keep forming as long as ATP is available. (b) Contracted: Z lines closer, I band narrower, H zone narrower or absent, A band unchanged.
items.markingKey: (a) stays contracted [1]; Ca²⁺ stays bound to troponin [1]; binding sites exposed [1] [3] (b) I band [1]; H zone [1]; A band unchanged [1] [3]

items.stem: Coleoptile sections grow faster in a buffer at pH 5 than at pH 7 with no auxin. What does this support?
options: Auxin is destroyed at low pH
Cell division is stimulated by alkaline pH
items.answer: The acid growth hypothesis
items.markingKey: Low pH activates expansins.

items.stem: Chloe floated 10 mm sections cut from wheat coleoptiles in solutions of different auxin (IAA) concentrations for 24 hours in the dark, then measured their final lengths. Results table. IAA concentration / mg dm⁻³: 0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10. Mean increase in length / mm, trial 1: 0.8, 0.9, 1.8, 4.5, 4.5, 1.8; trial 2: 0.7, 0.9, 1.8, 4.5, 4.7, 1.9; trial 3: 0.7, 0.9, 1.8, 4.5, 4.3, 1.8. Calculate the mean mean increase in length at 0.1 mg dm⁻³.
items.answer: 4.5 mm

items.stem: Kwame floated 10 mm sections cut from wheat coleoptiles in solutions of different auxin (IAA) concentrations for 24 hours in the dark, then measured their final lengths. Results table. IAA concentration / mg dm⁻³: 0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10. Mean increase in length / mm, trial 1: 0.9, 1.3, 2, 5, 4.7, 2; trial 2: 0.9, 0.9, 2, 4.9, 4.8, 2; trial 3: 0.9, 0.9, 2, 4.9, 4.9, 2. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Calculate the mean mean increase in length at 0.1 mg dm⁻³, ignoring any anomalous result.
items.answer: (a) Independent: IAA concentration; dependent: mean increase in length. (b) 4.93 mm
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = IAA concentration [1]; dependent variable = mean increase in length [1] [2] (b) (5 + 4.9 + 4.9) ÷ 3 [1] = 4.93 mm [1] [2]
